title: Our Environment
summary: Chapter 13: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current explores the relationship between electricity and magnetism. It covers magnetic field patterns around current-carrying conductors and solenoids, the right-hand thumb rule, Fleming's left-hand rule, and electromagnetic induction. The chapter explains electric motors, generators, and the domestic electric circuit with safety devices. Key concepts include magnetic field lines, the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, electromagnetic induction, and the working principle of transformers.

sections.heading: Magnetic Field and Field Lines
sections.para: The magnetic field is the region surrounding a magnet where its magnetic force can be detected. Magnetic field lines represent the magnetic field visually. They originate from the north pole and terminate at the south pole of a magnet. The density of field lines indicates the strength of the magnetic field. When electric current flows through a conductor, it produces a magnetic field around it. The pattern of magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying conductor consists of concentric circles centered on the conductor. The direction of the field lines depends on the direction of current flow, which can be determined using the right-hand thumb rule.
points: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed curves that emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole of a magnet.
The tangent to the magnetic field line at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field at that point.
No two magnetic field lines intersect each other as it would mean two different directions at the same point.
The magnetic field is stronger where the field lines are closer together and weaker where they are farther apart.
When current flows through a straight conductor, the magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the conductor.
The strength of the magnetic field increases with the increase in current and decreases with distance from the conductor.

keyTerms.meaning: The region around a magnet where its magnetic force can be detected
Imaginary lines used to represent the magnetic field around a magnet or current-carrying conductor
Rule to determine the direction of magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor

SI unit of magnetic field strength (1 T = 1 N/A·m)

sections.trick: Remember the right-hand thumb rule: 'Thumb shows current, fingers curl show field direction'. For magnetic field lines: 'North to south, outside the magnet; south to north, inside the magnet'.
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks questions on drawing magnetic field patterns around current-carrying conductors and solenoids. Expect 2-3 mark questions on right-hand thumb rule and Fleming's left-hand rule applications.

sections.heading: Magnetic Field due to a Current-Carrying Solenoid
sections.para: A solenoid is a long coil of wire wound in the form of a helix. When electric current passes through a solenoid, it behaves like a bar magnet with distinct north and south poles. The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform and parallel to its axis, while outside it resembles that of a bar magnet. The strength of the magnetic field inside a solenoid can be increased by increasing the number of turns per unit length, increasing the current flowing through it, or by inserting a soft iron core. The magnetic field lines inside the solenoid are straight and parallel, indicating a uniform magnetic field. The direction of the magnetic field can be determined using the right-hand thumb rule, where the thumb points in the direction of the current and the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.
points: A solenoid consists of a large number of turns of insulated wire wound in the form of a cylinder.
The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform and stronger than the field outside.
The magnetic field lines inside a solenoid are parallel to its axis.
The polarity of the solenoid depends on the direction of current flow through it.
Inserting a soft iron core in a solenoid increases its magnetic field strength many times.
The magnetic field strength of a solenoid is given by B = μ₀nI, where n is the number of turns per unit length.

keyTerms.meaning: A coil of wire wound in the form of a helix
A magnet made by passing current through a solenoid with a soft iron core
Property of a material that determines its magnetization in response to a magnetic field
Ratio of the magnetic permeability of a material to that of vacuum
Ability of a material to retain magnetization after the external field is removed
Resistance of a material to becoming demagnetized

sections.trick: Visualize a solenoid as a spring: 'Current flows through the wire, creating magnetic field lines like the spring's coils. Thumb points current direction, fingers curl field direction'.
sections.examPointer: Expect diagram-based questions on magnetic field patterns around solenoids. Questions on factors affecting magnetic field strength in solenoids often carry 2-3 marks. Remember to mention the effect of soft iron core.

sections.heading: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field
sections.para: When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. The magnitude of this force depends on the strength of the current, the length of the conductor in the magnetic field, the strength of the magnetic field, and the angle between the conductor and the field. The force is maximum when the conductor is perpendicular to the magnetic field and zero when it is parallel. The direction of the force can be determined using Fleming's left-hand rule. According to this rule, if the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field, the middle finger in the direction of current, then the thumb will point in the direction of the force experienced by the conductor. This principle is used in electric motors and other devices that convert electrical energy into mechanical energy.
points: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by F = BIL sinθ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field.
The force is maximum when θ = 90° (conductor perpendicular to the field) and zero when θ = 0° (conductor parallel to the field).
Fleming's left-hand rule helps determine the direction of the force on the conductor.
The force is perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field direction.
If the current is reversed, the force direction reverses.
If the magnetic field direction is reversed, the force direction reverses.

keyTerms.meaning: Force on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field
Rule to determine the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
SI unit of magnetic field strength (1 T = 1 N/A·m)
SI unit of electric current (1 A = 1 C/s)
SI unit of force (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²)
Conversion of electrical energy into mechanical energy using magnetic force

sections.trick: Remember Fleming's left-hand rule: 'First finger (Field), seCond finger (Current), thuMb (Motion). For F = BIL sinθ, maximum when sinθ = 1 (90°), zero when sinθ = 0 (0°).'
sections.examPointer: Numerical problems on force calculation are common. Expect 3-4 mark questions involving F = BIL sinθ with given values. Diagram-based questions on Fleming's left-hand rule frequently appear in exams.

sections.heading: Electric Motor
sections.para: An electric motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. It works on the principle that a current-carrying conductor experiences a force when placed in a magnetic field. The basic components of a simple electric motor include a coil of wire wound on a rotor, a permanent magnet to create the magnetic field, and a split-ring commutator to reverse the direction of current after every half rotation. As the current flows through the coil, it experiences a force according to Fleming's left-hand rule, causing the coil to rotate. The commutator ensures that the direction of current in the coil reverses after every half rotation, allowing continuous rotation in the same direction. The speed of rotation can be controlled by varying the current or the strength of the magnetic field. Motors are used in various applications like fans, washing machines, and electric vehicles.
points: An electric motor works on the principle that a current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field.
The force on the coil causes it to rotate continuously.
The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current after every half rotation.
The carbon brushes maintain electrical contact with the rotating commutator.
The speed of the motor can be increased by increasing the current or the magnetic field strength.
The direction of rotation can be reversed by reversing either the current direction or the magnetic field direction.

keyTerms.meaning: Device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy
A device that reverses the direction of current in the coil of a motor
The rotating part of an electric motor
The stationary part of an electric motor
Conducting brushes that maintain electrical contact with the commutator
Induced EMF that opposes the applied voltage in a motor

sections.trick: Remember: 'Current in, force out; commutator flips, spin about. Motor converts electrical to mechanical energy, Fleming's left hand shows the way.'
sections.examPointer: Expect questions on the principle, working, and components of electric motors. Diagram-based questions labeling parts of a motor are common. Questions on factors affecting motor speed and reversing direction often carry 2-3 marks.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic Induction
sections.para: Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating an electric current by moving a conductor through a magnetic field or by changing the magnetic field around a conductor. This phenomenon was discovered by Michael Faraday. The induced current is produced only when there is a relative motion between the conductor and the magnetic field. The magnitude of the induced current depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux, the number of turns in the coil, and the resistance of the circuit. The direction of the induced current can be determined using Fleming's right-hand rule. According to this rule, if the thumb points in the direction of motion, the first finger in the direction of the magnetic field, then the middle finger will point in the direction of the induced current. This principle is used in electric generators and transformers to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.
points: Electromagnetic induction was discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831.
An EMF is induced in a conductor when it moves through a magnetic field or when the magnetic field around it changes.
The induced EMF is given by ε = -dΦ/dt, where Φ is the magnetic flux.
Faraday's law states that the magnitude of induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
Lenz's law states that the direction of induced current opposes the change causing it.
The induced current is maximum when the conductor moves perpendicular to the magnetic field.

keyTerms.meaning: Process of generating an electric current by changing the magnetic field
Law stating that the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux
Law stating that the direction of induced current opposes the change causing it
Product of magnetic field strength and area perpendicular to the field (Φ = B·A·cosθ)
Electromotive force induced in a conductor due to changing magnetic field
Rule to determine the direction of induced current in a conductor

sections.trick: Remember: 'Change in flux, EMF induced; Lenz opposes, direction defined. Fleming's right hand: thumb motion, field first finger, current middle finger.'
sections.examPointer: Questions on Faraday's and Lenz's laws are common. Numerical problems on induced EMF calculation (ε = -dΦ/dt) often appear. Expect 3-4 mark questions on the principle of electromagnetic induction and its applications.

sections.heading: Electric Generator
sections.para: An electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. It consists of a coil of wire rotating between the poles of a magnet or a rotating magnet inside a stationary coil. As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux through it changes continuously, inducing an alternating current. The basic components of an AC generator include a coil, magnets, slip rings, and brushes. The slip rings maintain electrical contact with the rotating coil without reversing the current direction. In a DC generator, a split-ring commutator is used to convert the alternating current into direct current. The frequency of the alternating current depends on the speed of rotation and the number of poles in the generator. The magnitude of the induced voltage can be increased by increasing the number of turns in the coil, increasing the magnetic field strength, or increasing the speed of rotation.
points: An electric generator works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.
AC generators produce alternating current, while DC generators produce direct current.
The induced EMF in a rotating coil is given by ε = NBAω sinωt, where N is the number of turns, B is the magnetic field, A is the area, and ω is the angular velocity.
The frequency of AC is given by f = n/60, where n is the rotational speed in RPM.
Slip rings are used in AC generators to maintain electrical contact with the rotating coil.
A split-ring commutator is used in DC generators to convert AC to DC.

keyTerms.meaning: Generator that produces alternating current
Generator that produces direct current
Conducting rings that maintain electrical contact with a rotating part
A device that converts AC to DC in a generator
The coil in a generator that rotates in the magnetic field
The magnet that provides the magnetic field in a generator

sections.trick: Remember: 'Coil spins, flux changes, current induced. AC has rings, DC has split; both convert mechanical to electrical energy.'
sections.examPointer: Questions on the difference between AC and DC generators are common. Numerical problems on induced EMF calculation (ε = NBAω sinωt) often appear. Expect 3-4 mark questions on the principle, working, and components of generators.

sections.heading: Domestic Electric Circuits
sections.para: Domestic electric circuits are designed to safely distribute electrical power to various appliances in homes. They typically include live wire (red or brown), neutral wire (black or blue), and earth wire (green or yellow). The live wire carries the high voltage, the neutral wire completes the circuit, and the earth wire provides a path for fault current to the ground. Safety devices like fuses and circuit breakers protect against overloading and short circuits. A fuse is a safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when excessive current flows through it. A Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB) is a modern alternative that automatically switches off when current exceeds a safe limit. The power rating of appliances determines the current they draw, which must be within the safe capacity of the wiring. Parallel connections are used in domestic circuits to ensure that each appliance receives the full voltage and can operate independently.
points: Domestic circuits use a 220V AC supply with a frequency of 50Hz in India.
The live wire carries the high voltage (220V), the neutral wire completes the circuit, and the earth wire provides safety grounding.
Fuses and MCBs protect against overloading and short circuits.
A fuse melts when excessive current flows, breaking the circuit.
MCBs automatically switch off when current exceeds a safe limit.
Parallel connections ensure each appliance receives full voltage and operates independently.

keyTerms.meaning: Wire that carries the high voltage supply
Wire that completes the circuit and is at zero potential
Safety wire that provides a path for fault current to the ground
Safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when excessive current flows
Miniature Circuit Breaker that automatically switches off when current exceeds safe limit
A low-resistance connection between two conductors of different potentials

sections.trick: Remember: 'Red is live, black is neutral, green is earth for safety. Fuse blows, MCB trips, both protect from high current. Parallel connections keep voltage same across all devices.'
sections.examPointer: Questions on identifying live, neutral, and earth wires in diagrams are common. Expect 2-3 mark questions on the function of fuses and MCBs. Questions on advantages of parallel over series connections often appear.

sections.heading: Transformer
sections.para: A transformer is a device that changes the voltage of an alternating current without changing its frequency. It consists of two coils called primary and secondary wound on a common soft iron core. When an alternating current flows through the primary coil, it creates a changing magnetic field in the core, which induces an alternating current in the secondary coil. A step-up transformer increases the voltage from primary to secondary, while a step-down transformer decreases it. The voltage transformation ratio is equal to the turns ratio of the coils (Vs/Vp = Ns/Np). Transformers work on the principle of electromagnetic induction and are used in power transmission to reduce energy losses. The efficiency of a transformer is given by the ratio of output power to input power. Ideal transformers have 100% efficiency, but practical transformers have some losses due to resistance in coils, hysteresis in the core, and eddy currents.
points: A transformer works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.
It consists of two coils (primary and secondary) wound on a soft iron core.
The voltage transformation ratio is Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, where Vs and Vp are secondary and primary voltages, and Ns and Np are the number of turns in secondary and primary coils.
A step-up transformer increases voltage (Ns > Np), while a step-down transformer decreases voltage (Ns < Np).
Transformers are used in power transmission to reduce energy losses.
The efficiency of a transformer is given by η = (output power)/(input power) × 100%.

keyTerms.meaning: Device that changes the voltage of an alternating current
Input coil of a transformer connected to the AC supply
Output coil of a transformer connected to the load
Transformer that increases voltage from primary to secondary
Transformer that decreases voltage from primary to secondary
Current induced in a conductor when exposed to a changing magnetic field

sections.trick: Remember: 'More turns, more voltage; fewer turns, less voltage. Primary in, secondary out; iron core helps the flux about. Transformers change voltage, not frequency or power (ideally).'
sections.examPointer: Questions on the principle and working of transformers are common. Numerical problems on voltage transformation (Vs/Vp = Ns/Np) often appear. Expect 3-4 mark questions on step-up and step-down transformers and their applications.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic Waves
sections.para: Electromagnetic waves are waves that consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation. They do not require a medium for propagation and travel at the speed of light in vacuum (3 × 10^8 m/s). The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays, and gamma rays, arranged in order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength. Each type of electromagnetic wave has different applications based on its properties. Radio waves are used for communication, microwaves for cooking and radar, infrared for remote controls and thermal imaging, visible light for vision, ultraviolet for sterilization and vitamin D synthesis, X-rays for medical imaging, and gamma rays for cancer treatment and sterilization.
points: Electromagnetic waves consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other.
They travel at the speed of light in vacuum (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s).
The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.
The frequency and wavelength are related by c = fλ.
Different electromagnetic waves have different applications based on their properties.
Electromagnetic waves exhibit wave properties like reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of a redox reaction?
mcqs.explanation: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O is a redox reaction because hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced. In the other reactions, there is no change in oxidation states.

mcqs.question: The pH of a solution is 6. This solution is
mcqs.explanation: A pH value less than 7 indicates an acidic solution. Therefore, a solution with pH 6 is acidic.

mcqs.question: Which compound is commonly known as baking soda?
mcqs.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) is commonly known as baking soda. It is used in baking as a leavening agent.

mcqs.question: The chemical formula of bleaching powder is
mcqs.explanation: Bleaching powder is represented by the chemical formula CaOCl2, which is calcium oxychloride.

mcqs.question: Plaster of Paris is obtained by heating
mcqs.explanation: Plaster of Paris is obtained by heating gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) to about 373K. It is calcium sulfate hemihydrate (CaSO4·0.5H2O).

mcqs.question: Water of crystallisation in copper sulfate pentahydrate is
mcqs.explanation: Copper sulfate pentahydrate has the formula CuSO4·5H2O, indicating it contains 5 molecules of water of crystallisation.

mcqs.question: In the reactivity series, which metal is above hydrogen?
mcqs.explanation: Zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, meaning it can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper, gold, and silver are below hydrogen.

mcqs.question: The process of extracting metal from its ore is called
mcqs.explanation: Metallurgy is the process of extracting metals from their ores. It involves various steps like concentration, extraction, refining, etc.

mcqs.question: Thermite reaction is used for
mcqs.explanation: The thermite reaction (Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3) is highly exothermic and is used for welding railway tracks and other repair works.

mcqs.question: Which oxide is amphoteric?
mcqs.explanation: Aluminum oxide (Al2O3) is amphoteric, meaning it reacts with both acids and bases. Na2O is basic, MgO is basic, and SO2 is acidic.

mcqs.question: The bond formed by sharing of electrons is called
mcqs.explanation: A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms. Ionic bonds involve transfer of electrons, metallic bonds involve a sea of electrons, and hydrogen bonds are intermolecular forces.

mcqs.question: The first member of the homologous series of alkanes is
mcqs.explanation: Methane (CH4) is the first member of the homologous series of alkanes. The general formula for alkanes is CnH2n+2.

mcqs.question: The functional group present in ethanoic acid is
mcqs.explanation: Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) has the carboxyl functional group (-COOH), which is characteristic of carboxylic acids.

mcqs.question: The reaction between ethyl alcohol and ethanoic acid in the presence of an acid catalyst is called
mcqs.explanation: Esterification is the reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water. Ethyl alcohol and ethanoic acid undergo esterification to form ethyl acetate.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable pollutant?
mcqs.explanation: Plastic bags are non-biodegradable pollutants, meaning they cannot be broken down by natural processes. Fruit peels, vegetable waste, and paper are biodegradable.

mcqs.question: The process by which soap micelles remove dirt from clothes is called
mcqs.explanation: Emulsification is the process by which soap micelles surround and remove dirt particles by forming an emulsion with water. The dirt particles are trapped in the micelles and washed away.

mcqs.question: The main function of haemoglobin in blood is to transport
mcqs.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to the tissues where it is released. It also helps in transporting some carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

mcqs.question: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is
mcqs.explanation: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. It is responsible for filtering blood and forming urine.

mcqs.question: The part of the brain that controls balance and posture is
mcqs.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements, maintains balance, and ensures proper posture. The cerebrum is responsible for thinking, the medulla controls vital functions, and the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis.

mcqs.question: The hormone secreted by the pancreas that regulates blood sugar levels is
mcqs.explanation: Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the pancreas and helps in lowering blood sugar levels by promoting glucose uptake by cells. Glucagon raises blood sugar levels.

mcqs.question: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower is called
mcqs.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. Fertilization is the fusion of male and female gametes after pollination.

mcqs.question: The male reproductive organ in humans is called
mcqs.explanation: The testes are the male reproductive organs that produce sperm and the hormone testosterone. The ovaries are female reproductive organs, the uterus is where the embryo develops, and the fallopian tubes are where fertilization occurs.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of corrosion and how it can be prevented.
boardQuestions.answer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of materials (usually metals) by chemical reaction with their environment. It is an electrochemical process that involves the oxidation of metal atoms. For example, iron corrodes to form rust (iron oxide). Corrosion can be prevented by several methods: 1) Painting or coating the metal to prevent contact with air and moisture. 2) Galvanization, which involves coating iron with a layer of zinc. Zinc acts as a sacrificial anode and corrodes instead of iron. 3) Alloying the metal with other elements to make it more resistant to corrosion, such as stainless steel which contains chromium. 4) Using sacrificial protection where a more reactive metal is attached to the metal to be protected. 5) Electroplating with a less reactive metal like chromium or nickel.

boardQuestions.question: What are soaps and detergents? Explain their cleansing action.
boardQuestions.answer: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (fatty acids). They are made by the saponification reaction between fats or oils and an alkali like sodium hydroxide. Detergents are ammonium or sulphonate salts of long-chain hydrocarbons. They are synthetic cleansing agents. Both soaps and detergents have a hydrophilic (water-attracting) head and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) tail. When used for cleaning, the hydrophobic tails attach to dirt or grease particles, while the hydrophilic heads remain in water. This forms micelles where the dirt particles are trapped in the center, surrounded by the hydrophobic tails. The micelles are then washed away with water, effectively removing the dirt from the surface.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of nutrition in human beings.
boardQuestions.answer: Nutrition in human beings involves the process by which food is taken in, broken down, and used by the body for growth, repair, and energy. The process includes ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, and egestion. Ingestion is the intake of food. Digestion begins in the mouth where mechanical breakdown occurs by chewing and chemical breakdown by salivary amylase. In the stomach, food is mixed with gastric juices containing HCl and pepsin, which breaks down proteins. The food then enters the small intestine where complete digestion occurs with the help of pancreatic juices (containing trypsin, amylase, lipase) and intestinal juices (containing erepsin, maltase, lactase, lipase). Bile from the liver emulsifies fats. Absorption of nutrients occurs in the small intestine, which has villi to increase surface area. The absorbed nutrients are then assimilated into cells for various functions. Undigested food is egested through the anus.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the structure and function of the human heart.
boardQuestions.answer: The human heart is a muscular organ about the size of a fist, located in the chest cavity between the lungs. It has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava, which then flows into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps this blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery for oxygenation. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins, which then flows into the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps this oxygenated blood to the rest of the body through the aorta. The heart has valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic) that ensure one-way flow of blood. The heart's pumping action is due to the rhythmic contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of its muscles, which is regulated by the sinoatrial node (natural pacemaker).

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of excretion in human beings.
boardQuestions.answer: Excretion is the process of eliminating metabolic waste products from the body. In humans, the primary excretory organ is the kidney. Each kidney contains numerous nephrons, which are the functional units. The nephron filters blood under high pressure in the glomerulus. The filtrate contains water, glucose, salts, urea, and other wastes. As this filtrate passes through the tubule, useful substances like glucose and salts are reabsorbed. The remaining fluid, now containing concentrated wastes, forms urine. Urine flows through the ureters to the bladder, where it is stored before being expelled through the urethra. Other excretory organs include the skin (sweat), lungs (carbon dioxide), and liver (bile pigments).

boardQuestions.question: Explain the structure and function of a neuron.
boardQuestions.answer: A neuron is the basic unit of the nervous system. It consists of a cell body (soma), dendrites, and an axon. The cell body contains the nucleus and cytoplasm. Dendrites are branched extensions that receive signals from other neurons or sensory receptors. The axon is a long extension that transmits signals away from the cell body to other neurons, muscles, or glands. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath that speeds up signal transmission. At the end of the axon are synaptic terminals that release neurotransmitters to pass signals to the next neuron. Neurons transmit electrical impulses (action potentials) along their length and communicate with other neurons at synapses through chemical signals.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the process of photosynthesis.
boardQuestions.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some other organisms convert light energy into chemical energy. It occurs in the chloroplasts of plant cells, specifically in the thylakoid membranes and the stroma. The process involves two main stages: the light-dependent reactions and the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle). In the light-dependent reactions, light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to split water molecules (photolysis), releasing oxygen and producing ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide from the air is fixed into organic compounds using the ATP and NADPH produced earlier. The overall equation for photosynthesis is: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of fertilization in flowering plants.
boardQuestions.answer: Fertilization in flowering plants is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote. It begins with pollination, where pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma. The pollen grain germinates and grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovule in the ovary. The generative cell in the pollen grain divides to form two male gametes (sperm cells). One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote, which develops into the embryo. The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm, which provides nutrition to the developing embryo. This process is called double fertilization and is unique to flowering plants.

boardQuestions.question: A 12V battery is connected to a resistor of 6 ohms. Calculate the current flowing through the circuit and the power consumed by the resistor.
boardQuestions.answer: Given: Voltage (V) = 12V, Resistance (R) = 6 ohms. We need to find current (I) and power (P). Using Ohm's law: V = I × R. Therefore, I = V / R = 12V / 6Ω = 2A. The current flowing through the circuit is 2 amperes. Power consumed by the resistor can be calculated using P = V × I. P = 12V × 2A = 24W. Therefore, the power consumed by the resistor is 24 watts.

boardQuestions.question: An object is placed at a distance of 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Calculate the image distance and magnification. Also, state the nature of the image formed.
boardQuestions.answer: Given: Object distance (u) = -30 cm (negative as per sign convention), Focal length (f) = -15 cm (negative for concave mirror). Using mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Substituting values: 1/(-15) = 1/v + 1/(-30). -1/15 = 1/v - 1/30. 1/v = -1/15 + 1/30 = -2/30 + 1/30 = -1/30. Therefore, v = -30 cm. The image distance is 30 cm on the same side as the object. Magnification (m) = -v/u = -(-30)/(-30) = -1. The magnification is -1, indicating the image is real, inverted, and same size as the object.

boardQuestions.question: A 100W electric bulb is used for 8 hours daily. Calculate the energy consumed in a month of 30 days in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
boardQuestions.answer: Given: Power (P) = 100W = 0.1kW, Time per day = 8 hours, Number of days = 30. Energy consumed per day = Power × Time = 0.1kW × 8h = 0.8kWh. Total energy consumed in 30 days = Energy per day × Number of days = 0.8kWh × 30 = 24kWh. Therefore, the energy consumed in a month of 30 days is 24 kilowatt-hours.

boardQuestions.question: A heater coil has a resistance of 100 ohms and is connected to a 220V supply. Calculate the current drawn by the heater and the heat produced in 2 minutes.
boardQuestions.answer: Given: Voltage (V) = 220V, Resistance (R) = 100 ohms, Time (t) = 2 minutes = 120 seconds. Using Ohm's law: V = I × R. Therefore, I = V / R = 220V / 100Ω = 2.2A. The current drawn by the heater is 2.2 amperes. Heat produced (H) can be calculated using H = I² × R × t. H = (2.2)² × 100 × 120 = 4.84 × 100 × 120 = 58080J. Therefore, the heat produced in 2 minutes is 58080 joules.
